description.value: The study used [11C]PIB-PET and [18F]FDG-PET to investigate amyloid positivity and neurodegeneration across mild probable AD, aMCI, and healthy control groups, including clinical-biomarker mismatches and sociodemographic parameters.

spans.text: We report herein findings of the a large multimodal neuroimaging investigation in a Latin-American megacity (São Paulo, Brazil) that applied both [11C]PIB-PET and [18F]FDG-PET imaging in subjects with the clinical diagnosis of probable AD [23] or aMCI, as well as in cognitively healthy older adults.

description.value: Elderly individuals were clinically classified as controls, aMCI, or mild probable AD and underwent multimodal PET imaging.

spans.text: Elderly individuals (N=108) clinically classified as controls (N=27), aMCI (N=43) or mild probable AD (N=38) were included.

The AD and aMCI cohorts were composed with the joint efforts of a broad collaborative project within our University Hospital, which includes three different referring clinical services, one of them based at the department of Neurology (60 recruited) and two at the department of Psychiatry (28 recruited).

definition.value: the proportion of amyloid positivity across probable AD, aMCI, and control groups

value: The proportion of positive [11C]PIB-PETs (A+) was higher in the probable AD group (76%) in comparison to both the aMCI (37%) and control groups (18%) (p<0.001).
Although there was a higher proportion of A+ individuals in the aMCI group in comparison to the control group, this difference did not reach statistical significance (p=0.097).

definition.value: the frequency of abnormal [18F]FDG-PET patterns across probable AD, aMCI, and control groups

value: The proportion of positive [18F]FDG-PETs ((N)+) was higher in the probable AD group (76%) in comparison to both the aMCI (26%) and control groups (4%) (p<0.001).
There was also a higher proportion of (N)+ individuals in the aMCI group in comparison to controls (p=0.018).

spans.text: Patients should present the following features: (a) a perception of cognitive decline in relation to a previous level (according to the participant and an informant); (b) deficits in one or more cognitive domains below the expected average for the age and education, with at least one of the domains being related to memory (amnestic impairment) [27]; (c) independence for daily activities; (d) absence of dementia; and (e) absence of significant vascular disease, trauma, or general medical conditions as the attributable cause of the cognitive deficit.
Patients with aMCI also underwent extensive neuropsychological evaluations as described above, and their diagnosis was based on the revised Petersen criteria [27, 28].
